draft.title: Reaction pathways
card: A reaction pathway is a series of reactions that turns a starting compound into a target compound. The product of one step becomes the reactant of the next.
Each step uses a known reaction that changes one functional group. Examples: an alkene and HBr give a haloalkane, and a haloalkane and water give an alcohol.
To make a primary amine, react a haloalkane with excess ammonia. To make a carboxylic acid, oxidise a primary alcohol using acidified dichromate or permanganate.
To plan a pathway, work backwards from the target. Ask which functional group is needed, and which reaction makes it from the group you have.
draft.remember: Plan a pathway by working backwards from the target, one functional group change per step.

a.q: Which pathway makes propanoic acid from propene?
opts: Add H2O to make propan-1-ol, then oxidise it
Add Br2 to make a dibromopropane, then add ammonia
Add H2 to make propane, then swap in a chlorine atom
Add HBr to make a bromopropane, then add excess ammonia
a.why: Propanoic acid is made by oxidising the primary alcohol propan-1-ol. The last option ends in an amine, not a carboxylic acid, because ammonia reacts with a haloalkane to make an amine.
a.clue: Which functional group is oxidised to give a carboxylic acid?

b.q: Dana wants to make ethylamine from ethene. Which two-step pathway should she use?
opts: Ethene and HBr give bromoethane, then excess ammonia
Ethene and H2O give ethanol, then acidified dichromate
Ethene and H2 give ethane, then ethane and water
Ethene and Br2 give dibromoethane, then acidified dichromate
b.why: Bromoethane reacts with excess ammonia to give the primary amine ethylamine. The ethanol option is tempting because it is a real pathway, but oxidising ethanol gives ethanoic acid, which is a carboxylic acid and not an amine.
b.clue: Work backwards: which compound reacts with ammonia to make an amine?

a.best: Add H2O to make propan-1-ol, then oxidise it

b.best: Ethene and HBr give bromoethane, then excess ammonia

problems.detail: Adding water to propene mainly gives propan-2-ol (Markovnikov), not propan-1-ol. Oxidising propan-2-ol gives propanone, not propanoic acid, so the intended pathway is chemically misleading. Use a symmetrical alkene, such as ethene to ethanoic acid, or start from propan-1-ol or 1-bromopropane.
Why (a) calls the amine-ending option 'the last option', but the options are in a random order and the last option shown is the H2 then chlorine pathway. Name the option by its content instead.

a.q: Which pathway makes propanoic acid from 1-bromopropane?
opts: Add water to make propan-1-ol, then oxidise it
Add excess ammonia to make propan-1-amine, then oxidise it
Add water to make propan-1-ol, then add excess ammonia
Oxidise it with dichromate, then add water to the product
a.why: Water turns the haloalkane into the primary alcohol propan-1-ol, and oxidising a primary alcohol gives a carboxylic acid. The option that adds excess ammonia first is tempting, but it makes an amine, and only a primary alcohol is oxidised to a carboxylic acid.
a.clue: Which functional group is oxidised to give a carboxylic acid?

problems.detail: Why (a) says "only a primary alcohol is oxidised to a carboxylic acid". The card does not say "only", and it is not strictly true, since aldehydes also oxidise to carboxylic acids. Reword to "oxidising a primary alcohol gives a carboxylic acid".
Question b uses the common name "ethylamine", while question a uses the IUPAC name "propan-1-amine". VCE expects IUPAC naming, so use "ethanamine" (or give both) to stay consistent.
